Mitla invites you to take a closer look at its walls. The palaces of this ancient Zapotec center are decorated with geometric mosaics made from small, carefully worked stones. Stepped lines, turns and repeating patterns cover entire panels. When light falls from the side, the precision of the joints and the depth of the designs become especially apparent.

The archaeological site lies in the town of San Pablo Villa de Mitla in the Oaxaca Valley. It preserves several groups of buildings, courtyards and passages between them. In the Hall of Columns, each support was carved from a single block of stone. Some areas offer a glimpse of how the palace spaces were arranged and how important wall decoration was.

Mitla appeals to anyone interested in architecture and the craftsmanship of ancient builders. Take your time among the ornaments: compare neighboring panels, notice the different motifs and look for surviving traces of red paint. The modern town surrounds the ancient structures, making it easy to continue exploring the region's living culture after visiting the archaeological site.

Mixquic is known for its Day of the Dead traditions. During the celebration, families decorate altars and graves with flowers, candles and objects associated with loved ones who have died. Remembering family members here takes the form of gathering together, sharing food and caring for burial places.

The community offers a more intimate introduction to local customs alongside Mexico City's large celebrations. Festive displays include photographs and personal belongings that tell the stories of individual people. Mixquic shows how a shared Mexican tradition lives on in the everyday lives of a particular community and its families.
